Inflammation is on a continuum, and establishing a serum ferritin threshold for the diagnosis of iron deficiency is challenging. However, in adults with anemia of inflammation, the diagnosis of iron deficiency may be considered when (1) TSAT <20% or (2) serum ferritin <100 ng/mL.

TSAT should be drawn in a fasting state (5-9 hours, including fasting from multivitamin or iron supplements) because the test is susceptible to recent dietary intake.

Anemia of inflammation may occur in individuals with inflammatory bowel disease, infectious diseases, cancer, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, rheumatologic disorders, and other inflammatory disorders.

Because of a lack of data on the diagnosis of iron deficiency in children with inflammation, no recommendations were made for this population (see recommendation 1).

Good practice statement

Anemia of inflammation may be present concurrently with other causes of anemia. Consequently, in individuals with inflammation, serum ferritin and TSAT should be analyzed in context of the full clinical picture, including consideration of the history, physical exam, underlying disease process, and other existing management guidelines, for chronic diseases. Such guidelines may consider higher serum ferritin and/or TSAT thresholds for the diagnosis of iron deficiency.

Evidence for diagnostic test accuracy included 2 comparative cross-sectional studies of individuals (n = 67),; 1 study included adults with heart failure, and 1 study included adults with renal failure. Both studies presented data on the sensitivity and specificity comparing serum ferritin alone vs performing both serum ferritin and TSAT. The pooled sensitivity and specificity for serum ferritin alone (<100 ng/mL) were 0.38 and 0.88, respectively. For serum ferritin threshold <100 ng/mL and/or TSAT <20%, the pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.91 and 0.70, respectively. Supplemental 9 provides the evidence profile and EtD framework for recommendation 5.

The accurate diagnosis of iron deficiency in the setting of inflammation allows for the potential initiation of therapy to mitigate the negative consequences of iron deficiency, which include worsening of anemia and exacerbation of poorer outcomes related to the underlying comorbid condition and primary cause of inflammation. The diagnosis of absolute iron deficiency can be challenging in the presence of inflammation because serum ferritin may be falsely “normal” or “elevated” because it is an acute-phase reactant. Therefore, panel members considered assessment of serum ferritin alone as often insufficient to assess iron status in adults with inflammation and supported the use of multiple iron parameters to inform the diagnosis. TSAT reflects circulating iron and identifies states of iron-restricted erythropoiesis, irrespective of the presence of inflammation, thereby providing additional information to inform the individual’s iron status.

The panel considered serum ferritin <100 ng/mL or TSAT <20% to be accurate for the diagnosis of iron deficiency for many, but not necessarily all, individuals in the setting of inflammation. The panel recognized that inflammation is a continuum and that dichotomous thresholds are limited in fully characterizing the spectrum and range of inflammation. Regardless, thresholds for diagnostic and treatment guidance were judged to be of moderate benefit to patients.

To determine the undesirable effects of using serum ferritin alone vs serum ferritin or TSAT to make a diagnosis of iron deficiency in adults with inflammation, the panel considered false-positive and false-negative diagnoses. The panel considered the undesirable effects of unnecessary iron therapy in persons falsely identified to be deficient and the negative health consequences of missing the diagnosis of iron deficiency, which would include worse fatigue, impaired cognition, poorer health-related quality of life, and worse outcomes related to the comorbid illness (false negatives). The panel prioritized the desire to minimize false negatives and considered the undesirable effects of using serum ferritin ≤100 ng/mL alone to be moderate and those of using serum ferritin ≤100 ng/mL or TSAT <20% overall to be likely to be small. Panel members expressed their willingness to give iron treatment when TSAT was ≤20% even if anemia might be because of iron-restricted erythropoiesis rather than absolute iron deficiency because of the potential for positive health benefits for both conditions.

Certainty in the evidence of test accuracy was judged to be low because of concerns around the risk of bias and the use of indirect evidence. For instance, in evaluating management effects, the panel considered indirect evidence from 4 randomized controlled trials in individuals with iron deficiency and heart failure that defined iron deficiency as serum ferritin ≤100 ng/mL or TSAT <20%.,, , All 4 trials showed consistent improvement in symptoms, with very few reported side effects. The panel acknowledged that because of the presence of chronic comorbid conditions and inflammation, although individuals may have improvement in symptoms with IV iron, resolution of anemia may not be complete (because of other contributing causes of anemia) even after treatment with IV iron. The panel posits that most individuals would value being aware of having absolute or functional iron deficiency, although individuals may vary in their prioritization of receiving treatment for iron deficiency in the setting of other comorbidities. Despite variations in costs and charges of the laboratory tests, the panel considered the difference between serum ferritin alone and serum ferritin and TSAT to likely be of negligible costs and savings. The panel assessed the testing to likely be acceptable to patients and feasible for providers.

Given the difficulty of diagnosing absolute iron deficiency in individuals with inflammation, and acknowledging that inflammation is a continuum, a variety of tests have been proposed to supplement the diagnosis. These included the use of sTfR or markers of inflammation, such as sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein, to “adjust” serum ferritin threshold for inflammation. In reviewing these potential adjunctive tests, none had sufficient data to recommend their use as standalone tests, but they may be helpful in the full context of the individual’s clinical condition and other laboratory values.

The guideline panel suggests assessment of both serum ferritin and TSAT for the diagnosis of iron deficiency in adults with inflammation despite a low certainty in the evidence for a net health benefit and harm reduction.

Based on available evidence, serum ferritin of <100 ng/mL or TSAT <20% may identify many individuals with concomitant iron deficiency in the setting of inflammation, thereby reducing untreated iron deficiency and its attendant negative health consequences. Because of the low certainty in the evidence and the very limited number of prospective trials providing indirect evidence, a recommendation regarding specific thresholds was not made.

The panel identified the following additional research questions in individuals with inflammation:1.Studies on various iron parameters, including diagnostic hepcidin assays, to inform the diagnosis of iron deficiency in the setting of anemia of inflammation.2.Evaluation of the relationship between serum ferritin and TSAT in pediatrics, including the optimal threshold for diagnosing iron deficiency in children with concomitant inflammation.3.Randomized clinical trials that examine different iron parameters for the diagnosis of iron deficiency in individuals with inflammation to guide treatment and assess patient-important outcomes.

sections.title: What are others saying, and what is new in these guidelines?
sections.text:
Guidance from the WHO recommends a serum ferritin threshold of <12 ng/mL for children and a threshold of <15 ng/mL for otherwise healthy adults. These thresholds are considered highly specific but have low sensitivity for the accurate diagnosis of individuals with iron deficiency. Evidence assessed by this guideline panel examined these specific ranges and identified low evidence to suggest the use of these thresholds in any population.

A new joint clinical report on iron deficiency and iron deficiency anemia from the AAP and the American Society of Pediatric Hematology/Oncology will provide diagnostic guidance for infants, children, and adolescents that is consistent with the serum ferritin thresholds developed in these ASH diagnostic guidelines. The American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology recommends a serum ferritin threshold of <30 ng/mL for the diagnosis of iron deficiency in pregnant people. The National Bleeding Disorder Foundation Medical and Scientific Advisory Council 2026 guidelines recommend a ferritin level of <50 ng/mL as the cutoff for diagnosing iron deficiency in males and females with inherited bleeding disorders at all ages.

sections.title: Call to action on screening
sections.text:
Recommendations on screening were out of scope of this diagnostic guideline because of the need to prioritize diagnostic thresholds to facilitate accurate diagnosis across populations. Therefore, an evidence-based review focused on screening for iron deficiency was not performed.

Since 2010, the AAP has recommended universal anemia screening in young children at the age of 12 months. A joint clinical report from the AAP and the American Society of Pediatric Hematology/Oncology published in 2026 recommends universal screening for both anemia and iron deficiency in all young children as well as all menstruating individuals after the onset of menarche. The National Bleeding Disorder Foundation Medical and Scientific Advisory Council 2026 guidelines include recommendations for screening all individuals with inherited bleeding disorders for iron deficiency and anemia. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists does not currently recommend routine screening for iron deficiency during pregnancy. However, a body of evidence demonstrates the pervasiveness of iron deficiency (defined as serum ferritin <30 ng/mL) in pregnancy irrespective of the presence or absence of anemia. In addition to affecting maternal outcomes, iron deficiency has potential negative impacts on the developing fetus. The use of hemoglobin and mean corpuscular volume as surrogates for iron sufficiency is inaccurate, and literature demonstrates positive effects of early iron repletion in nonanemic pregnant individuals., , Based on the preceding statements, the panel believes it is reasonable to screen for iron deficiency by checking serum ferritin in all pregnant individuals as well as other high-risk populations with or without concomitant anemia.

sections.title: Limitations of these guidelines
sections.text: The limitations of these guidelines are inherent in the low or very low certainty in the evidence we identified for many of the questions.

sections.title: Revision or adaptation of the guidelines
sections.text:
After publication of these guidelines, ASH will maintain them through surveillance for new evidence, ongoing review by experts, and regular revisions.

Although a global perspective was taken in the development of this guideline, adaptation of these guidelines will be necessary in many circumstances. These adaptations should be based on the associated EtD frameworks.
